newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan pledges $1.1 bln in new aid to Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Japan pledges $1.1 bln in new aid to Philippines.

text.p: Japan announced a new yen loan package worth 124.3 billion yen ($1.11 billion) for the Philippines in talks on Sunday between Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and President Fidel Ramos, Japanese officials said.

The new aid package, to be disbursed within a year, covers 14 development projects, including those at Subic Bay and the southern island of Mindanao, said a senior Japanese foreign ministry official who took part in the Hashimoto-Ramos talks. The two met in Manila ahead of a summit of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Subic Bay on Monday.
Ramos promised to revise a domestic law which had restricted engineers and building contractors in aid-related projects, the Japanese official said.
The aid package covers two projects on Mindanao. One is to improve a highway on the island and the other a flood-control project of the lower reaches of the Agusan river.
It also covers a plan to improve the Subic Bay free port, the Japanese official said.
Besides the 14 projects, Japan will also start drafting a plan to overhaul the Subic Bay area as part of future aid packages. This is a larger project than improving the free port, the official said.

Hashimoto also promised to send Japanese fruit inspectors to Mindanao to boost the export of papaya fruit to Japan. Inspectors were not sent earlier because of continued activities by Moslem guerrillas.
The Japanese decision on the Mindanao projects and the inspectors came after Ramos signed a peace agreement with the main Moslem rebel group, the Moro National Liberation Front, in September.
Ramos thanked Hashimoto for the aid package and said he was especially happy about the projects on Mindanao, the Japanese official said.

The Philippine government is trying to drum up foreign investment in the southern island in the hope that a taste of the prosperity the rest of the country is enjoying will discourage a return to violence by the rebels.

Hashimoto also asked for Ramos's support for the U.S.-proposed Information Technology Agreement (ITA), a plan to seek the elimination of tariffs on computers and related goods through the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
The ITA is one of the biggest issues at the Subic Bay APEC summit, along with China's proposed entry into the WTO.
Ramos only replied that he understood the importance of the ITA, the Japanese official said.
